definition: The standard subjective quality measures for synthesized speech: absolute 1-5 naturalness ratings (MOS) or side-by-side comparative ratings (CMOS).
details: The standard subjective quality measures for synthesized speech: absolute 1-5 naturalness ratings (MOS) or side-by-side comparative ratings (CMOS). Human MOS remains the gold standard; neural predictors (UTMOS-style) approximate it cheaply at scale.

explainer.lead: MOS and CMOS are ways of asking people how good synthesized speech sounds. MOS collects absolute naturalness ratings on a 1–5 scale, while CMOS uses side-by-side comparisons, giving speech researchers a human quality measure that automated predictions only approximate.

tiers.eli5: Imagine several people making robot voices and asking you to judge them. With MOS, you give each voice a naturalness score from 1 to 5; with CMOS, you listen to voices next to each other and compare them. Averaging people’s judgments gives a better picture than relying on one person’s ears.
tiers.practitioner: Use human MOS for absolute 1–5 naturalness evaluation and CMOS when listeners compare synthesized speech side by side. UTMOS-style neural predictors can approximate human MOS cheaply at scale, but their predictions should not be treated as the human gold standard.
tiers.paperLevel: MOS is the mean of listeners’ absolute naturalness ratings on a 1–5 scale: MOS = (r1 + r2 + ... + rn) / n. CMOS instead uses comparative ratings collected from side-by-side listening. Human MOS remains the gold standard; UTMOS-style neural predictors are scalable approximations with that fundamental limitation.

explainer.example: Listeners give synthesized voice A naturalness ratings of 4, 5, and 4, producing a MOS of 4.33. In a separate side-by-side CMOS test, they compare voice A with voice B and provide comparative ratings rather than judging either voice only in isolation.

usedIn.name: Synthesized-speech evaluation
usedIn.detail: Listeners provide absolute MOS naturalness ratings or comparative CMOS judgments.

usedIn.name: UTMOS-style quality prediction
usedIn.detail: Neural models approximate human MOS to estimate speech quality cheaply at scale.

explainer.intuition: The most direct way to judge whether synthetic speech sounds natural is to ask people to listen and rate it. MOS summarizes isolated ratings, whereas CMOS captures comparisons between alternatives.
howItWorks: Prepare synthesized speech samples for listeners to hear.
For MOS, ask each listener to rate a sample’s naturalness from 1 to 5.
Average the collected ratings to obtain the MOS.
For CMOS, present samples side by side and collect comparative ratings.
Optionally use a UTMOS-style neural predictor to approximate MOS when human evaluation at scale would be costly.
explainer.whyItMatters: These measures connect speech-quality evaluation to human perception instead of relying solely on automated estimates. Human MOS is the gold standard, while neural prediction makes large-scale approximation cheaper.
misconceptions: MOS and CMOS are not the same procedure: MOS uses absolute 1–5 ratings, while CMOS uses side-by-side comparative ratings.
A neural MOS prediction is not itself human MOS; it is an approximation of the gold standard.

diagram.caption: Human listening produces absolute MOS or comparative CMOS judgments; a neural predictor offers a cheaper MOS approximation.
